title: The Postcard of Junebug Creek Anew
premise: After a humiliating onstage collapse, cellist Edmund Quintana retreats to Junebug Creek to teach at a summer arts festival, where a community pen-pal program meant to heal old town feuds accidentally pairs him with Marisol Vega — the festival director whose testimony once ended his career. Writing anonymously under assigned numbers, they confess truths neither could say face-to-face, falling for the stranger while sparring as enemies by day. When the letters' authorship is exposed before the closing festival concert, Edmund must choose between protecting his pride and publicly defending Marisol against the board trying to oust her. He plays the performance he once failed, dedicating it to her, and they choose the whole heart over safe, rationed pieces of one.
about_author: P. M. Eastwick is the pen name of a former orchestra librarian who spent a decade backstage watching musicians fall in and out of love with their art. Now writing from a porch overlooking a creek not unlike Junebug's, Eastwick crafts romances about second chances and the courage of unguarded hearts.

chapters.title: The Assignment
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Arriving in Junebug Creek with a damaged cello and a damaged reputation, Edmund clashes instantly with festival director Marisol Vega, who he blames for his downfall. The town's pen-pal program assigns them anonymous numbers by clerical error. Emotional beat: wounded pride masking loneliness; he writes his first letter out of spite and surprises himself with honesty.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Creek
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. By day, Edmund and Marisol battle over the festival program; by night, their letters deepen into confession — she reveals the pressure she was under when she testified against him, he admits the collapse was panic, not sabotage. Emotional beat: loyalty to old grievances vs. growing truth; each begins suspecting, then dreading, who the stranger might be.

chapters.title: What the Board Saw
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. A rival board member intercepts and publishes the letters, exposing them both and framing Marisol's judgment as compromised to force her removal before the festival ends. Edmund, humiliated publicly a second time, nearly flees — until he realizes staying silent would betray her as others once betrayed him. Emotional beat: climax of choice; justice outside the law means defending her without a contract, a stage, or permission.

chapters.title: The Whole Heart
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, closing with both. At the final concert, Edmund takes the stage uninvited, names what happened three years ago, and plays the piece that broke him — dedicating it to the woman the letters taught him to trust. The town rallies to reinstate Marisol. Emotional beat: resolution; belonging earned not through safety but through risk, and two enemies choosing love with nothing held back.
